analysis.one_liner: Requires giant social media platforms to let users move their data to rival services.
analysis.headline: Despite sponsorship from two Senate Democrats and two Senate Republicans, the bill was referred to committee in May 2022 and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require communications platforms with more than 100 million U.S. monthly users to build interfaces that let users take their data with them and let rival apps interconnect with platform users. Competitors and user-designated agents could access the data only to provide the service, not to resell it. The FTC would enforce the rules, with each affected user counting as a separate violation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology would publish model technical standards for messaging, photo sharing, and social networking.
analysis.who_benefits: Social media users who want to leave a dominant platform without abandoning their photos, contacts, and message history, and the smaller companies trying to serve them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social media users and rival apps

how_it_helps.text: Requires platforms with more than 100 million monthly U.S. users to maintain transparent interfaces so users can transfer their data, in a structured, machine-readable format, to themselves or to a competing service acting for them.
Requires those platforms to maintain interoperable interfaces so users of competing services can communicate with users of the large platform, on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory terms.
Prohibits competitors and the platforms themselves from using data obtained through the interoperability interface for commercial purposes, limiting it to privacy, security, and interoperability.

Directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to publish model technical standards within 180 days for online messaging, multimedia sharing, and social networking, and requires the FTC to write implementation regulations.
Allows the FTC to treat each affected user as an individual violation when fining a breach of the rules, and to register and deregister third-party agents that manage accounts on users' behalf.

analysis.who_pays: The dominant platforms, which would have to build and maintain open interfaces and give up part of the lock-in that keeps users from leaving; users of delegated account services could face fees from those agents.

drawbacks.text: Opening data-transfer channels creates new privacy and security risk: competitors receiving ported user data are required only to 'reasonably secure' it, and custodial third-party agents with access to users' accounts are a new point of failure.

Platforms are allowed to set reasonable thresholds and charge fees for high-volume access to interoperability interfaces, and custodial third-party agents may charge users a fee for managing their accounts, so some of the benefit could come with new costs.

Compliance hinges on FTC rulemaking and enforcement: the law would take effect only after the FTC promulgates regulations, and enforcement runs through the FTC rather than giving users a direct way to sue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and structural: users keep their data and connections when they switch, which weakens the network effects that make dominant platforms hard to leave. The security and fee concerns are genuine but addressable through the NIST standards and FTC rules the bill itself sets up; the larger weakness is that the whole scheme depends on an FTC that would have to write detailed rules and police a handful of the world's largest companies.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2022 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which took no further action on it before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner introduced the bill on May 25, 2022 with four original cosponsors: Democrats Blumenthal and Klobuchar and Republicans Graham and Hawley.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no markup, vote, or floor action followed for the rest of the Congress.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill advancing out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large social media platforms, which kept the data and network lock-in the bill would have required them to open up; users and would-be competitors gained nothing.

industries.industry: Large social media and messaging platforms (100M+ U.S. users)
industries.note: The bill would force them to open their user data and connect with rivals on nondiscriminatory terms, eroding the lock-in that keeps users from switching. Platforms may charge fees for heavy access, but the core obligation runs against their current business model.

industries.industry: Rival and emerging platforms and app startups
industries.note: They would get documented interfaces, interoperability rights, and access to ported user data, provided they secure it and do not commercialize it. Easier switching means a real chance to win users.

The bill creates a new FTC-registered class of firms authorized to manage users' accounts and data on their behalf, and lets them charge users a fee. Their duties to safeguard data run in the user's favor.
